statement: The one study read here that counted birth defects after ecstasy use in pregnancy is a letter from a UK teratology information service, a prospective case series with no comparison group (it cites an interim report of 92 pregnancies from the same service and a Dutch series of 43, neither of which was read). From 302 enquiries (1989 to June 1998) it followed 136 pregnancies in which ecstasy was used (74 ecstasy only, 62 with other drugs, nearly all in the first 3 months); 135 enquiries (45%) were lost to follow-up and 31 (10%) had not finished. Of the 136, 11 ended in miscarriage and 48 in elective termination, and the other 77 gave 78 live-born infants (one pair of twins); 12 of the 78 (15.4%, 95% CI 8.2 to 25.4) had a congenital anomaly, which the authors call significantly higher than an expected 2 to 3% (no test is reported, the benchmark has no source, and the list includes minor findings such as a toe lying under its neighbour, a flat spot on the head, a drooping eyelid and clicking hips). Two infants had heart defects (26 per 1000 live births), both also exposed to other drugs by the table's grouping, and three girls had talipes (38 per 1000), all in the ecstasy-only group by the table's grouping; the authors say the series has too little statistical power to confirm a causal link with any anomaly, and no effect on the sex ratio was seen (McElhatton et al., 1999). A later cohort of 28 exposed women did not report a count of anomalies; one exposed infant had a rare genetic syndrome (Townes-Brocks), a spontaneous mutation that the authors say cannot be attributed specifically to maternal drug exposure (Singer et al., 2012). That cohort paper describes the 1999 letter as showing a 4 to 7 times higher risk, and a two-fold risk after allowing for higher-risk pregnancies; the letter prints neither figure and makes no such adjustment (editors' calculation: 15.4% against an expected 2 to 3% is a ratio of about 5 to 8).
plain: One study counted birth defects after ecstasy use in pregnancy. A UK information service followed 136 pregnancies. Of 78 babies born alive, 12 (about 15 in 100) had a birth defect, a mix of minor and major ones, more than the 2 to 3 in 100 the authors expected. But there was no comparison group, almost half of the enquiries were lost to follow-up, and 62 of the 136 pregnancies also involved other drugs. So the study cannot show whether ecstasy changes the chance of a birth defect. A later study followed babies of 28 women who used ecstasy but did not report a count of birth defects.
population: Women who used ecstasy in pregnancy and whose health professionals enquired to a UK teratology information service (136 pregnancies, 78 live births), and a cohort of 96 women of whom 28 used MDMA in the month before or during pregnancy
exposure: Self-reported ecstasy use in pregnancy, mostly in the first 3 months, alone (74 pregnancies) or with other drugs (62), reported second-hand by the enquirer; no doses or tablet contents
comparator: None in the case series (an unreferenced expected incidence of 2 to 3% was used); 68 comparison women in the cohort
outcome: Congenital anomalies in live-born infants, miscarriage, termination, prematurity, birth weight and sex ratio
magnitude: McElhatton et al. (1999): 12 of 78 live-born infants with an anomaly, 15.4% (95% CI 8.2 to 25.4), against an expected 2 to 3% (no source); congenital heart disease in 2 infants, 26 per 1000 live births (95% CI 3.0 to 90.0), against 5 to 10 per 1000; talipes in 3 infants, 38 per 1000 (95% CI 8 to 109), against 1 per 1000. Miscarriage 11 of 136 (8%), elective termination 48 (35%), 8 premature births, 1 neonatal death, 3 term infants under 2.5 kg, no effect on sex ratio. 45% of enquiries lost to follow-up. No comparison group, so no risk ratio can be calculated. Singer et al. (2012): 1 of 28 exposed infants with Townes-Brocks syndrome (spontaneous SALL1 mutation per the authors).

evidence.locator: Research letter, 3rd paragraph (the summary above the text counted as the 1st; begins 'The UK National Teratology Information Service')
evidence.extracted: The UK National Teratology Information Service followed up 136 pregnancies (one pair of twins) with ecstasy exposure from January 1989 to June 1998; there were 302 enquiries, of which 31 (10%) were not yet completed and 135 (45%) were lost to follow-up because the enquirer could no longer identify the patient or she did not return to the surgery.

evidence.locator: Research letter, 5th and 6th paragraphs (begin '74 pregnant women reported' and '127 women')
evidence.extracted: 74 women reported ecstasy only and 62 ecstasy with other drugs of abuse (amphetamine 37, cocaine 20, cannabis 16, alcohol 13, LSD nine, other 13); acute toxicity from ecstasy in two mothers. 127 women (71 ecstasy alone, 56 with other drugs) were exposed in the first trimester, two in the first and second, two in the second and one in the third; four were exposed to several drugs throughout pregnancy.

evidence.locator: Research letter, 7th and 8th paragraphs (begin '11 pregnancies resulted in miscarriage' and 'There were 78 liveborn infants'); summary above the text; Table (Malformations reported after exposure of fetus to ecstasy and other drugs of abuse)
evidence.extracted: 11 pregnancies ended in miscarriage (8%, within the expected range) and 48 in elective termination (35%, higher than the UK average; one after prenatal diagnosis of malformations); no necropsy data on the other aborted fetuses; by subtraction (editors' arithmetic) the other 77 pregnancies gave the 78 live-born infants, one pair being twins. 78 live-born infants: 66 normal and 12 with congenital anomalies, 15.4% (95% CI 8.2 to 25.4), described as significantly higher than an expected incidence of 2 to 3%, with no test or P value given; the summary calls this a possible association with a significantly increased risk of congenital defects; the table lists 13 anomaly findings (12 live-born, plus one terminated fetus with absent upper limbs), among them a toe under its neighbour, plagiocephaly, pyloric stenosis, ptosis, pigmentation of a thigh and clicking hips. No source is given for the expected incidence.
evidence.quote: may be associated with a significantly increased risk of congenital defects

evidence.locator: Research letter, 9th and 10th paragraphs (begin 'Eight infants were born prematurely' and 'No adverse effects were observed in the sex ratio')
evidence.extracted: Eight infants were born prematurely (25 to 36 weeks, including twins at 25 weeks; two fetal distress cases thought unrelated to ecstasy); one neonatal death in an infant of a mother who took ecstasy, heroin and methadone throughout pregnancy; no adverse effect on sex ratio; birthweights within the expected range for term infants, with only three under 2.5 kg.

evidence.locator: Research letter, 11th and 12th paragraphs (begin 'There were three female infants with talipes' and 'The spontaneous incidence of congenital heart disease'); summary above the text
evidence.extracted: Three female infants had talipes (38 per 1000, CI 8 to 109, against an expected 1 per 1000; the letter says idiopathic talipes is male-predominant 3 to 1 in the UK); two infants had congenital heart disease, ventricular septal defects (26 per 1000, CI 3.0 to 90.0, against an expected 5 to 10 per 1000). The authors say the small series has insufficient statistical power to confirm a causal relation with any particular anomaly but consider the data important. Editors' reading of the table: the three infants with talipes were in the ecstasy-only group, and both infants with a ventricular septal defect had other drug exposure.

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.2 Birth and Neonatal Child Outcomes, 2nd paragraph; 4. Discussion, 9th paragraph; Footnote 1
evidence.extracted: One infant in the MDMA-exposed group was diagnosed with Townes-Brocks syndrome, a rare genetic multiple-malformation syndrome of the gene SALL1, documented by genetic testing as a spontaneous (de novo) mutation; neither parent was a carrier. The authors say it would have occurred before conception and cannot be attributed specifically to maternal drug exposure; the mother had reported MDMA twice a month in the first trimester and none later, with cigarettes, alcohol and some cocaine. Results with and without this child did not differ. The paper does not report a count of other anomalies.

The Introduction describes the 1999 series of 136 pregnancies as indicating a 4 to 7 times higher risk of congenital malformations and a two-fold risk even after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies; the Discussion calls its 15.4% an increased risk, which echoes the letter's own summary. The letter reports a proportion (12 of 78 live births) compared informally with an unreferenced 2 to 3%, with no multiples printed, no adjusted analysis and no comparison group; it contains neither the 4 to 7 times nor the two-fold figure. Editors' calculation: 15.4% against an expected 2 to 3% is a ratio of about 5 to 8.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I critical on the study card: no comparison group, 45% of enquiries lost to follow-up, other drugs in 62 of 136 pregnancies, exposure and anomalies reported second-hand by the enquirer without definition or examination.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: one case series; the cohort does not count anomalies.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for what was reported to one service in the 1990s, not for current use or for tablet contents.

imprecision.note: Subgroup rates rest on 2 and 3 infants with intervals running from 3 to 90 and 8 to 109 per 1000.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim from a case series starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias -2 (critical, no comparison group) and imprecision -1 give very low. Status single-study. The claim is worded as insufficient evidence: the counts are reported with their limits, and the paper's own caution about statistical power is stated. It does not support a risk figure or a risk ratio, and the later cohort's mis-description of the letter is noted as a reporting error, not a finding.

verification.flag_note: Joins with the claim on infant development at 1 and 4 months (same exposure, different outcomes). The editor may keep them separate: the case series counts anomalies without a comparison, the cohort measures development with one.
